loText: Describe the practice of co-investing in private markets and assess its advantages and disadvantages.
question: Which of the following best describes the practice of co-investing in private markets?

options.A: A private investor invests directly in a specific deal alongside a private market fund, typically by invitation from the fund manager, generally at lower fees than investing through the fund itself; managers extend such opportunities when they need additional capital to complete a deal exceeding their usual investment limits, and access is usually restricted to large, established investors with whom the manager has a strong relationship.
options.B: Two or more fund managers pool their capital to acquire a target jointly, sharing carried interest between them, with limited partners participating only through their existing fund commitments.
options.C: A private investor purchases an existing limited partnership interest from another investor in the secondary market, thereby gaining exposure to a portfolio of deals already made.
options.D: A fund manager offers all limited partners a pro rata right to increase their exposure to any deal, which is exercised on a standardised timetable set out in the partnership agreement.

solution:
| Feature | Content |
|---|---|
| What it is | A private investor investing directly in a specific deal alongside a private market fund, typically by invitation from a fund manager. |
| Why the manager offers it | Managers extend co-investment opportunities when they need additional capital to complete a deal that exceeds their usual investment limits. |
| Who is invited | Access is usually restricted to large, established investors with whom the manager has a strong relationship. |
| How it arrives | Often on short notice, requiring accelerated due diligence and decision-making. Some managers also offer dedicated co-investment vehicles, which formalise access. |

Option (c) describes a secondary transaction, which is a different instrument named separately in this reading: co-investments  […]

loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured.
question:
An internal auditor at a fund of funds is checking the reporting-risk section of a quarterly review of four underlying buyout funds. All NAVs are determined by the respective fund managers, and some figures are missing from the table.

| Fund | TVPI (x) | DPI (x) | RVPI (x) | Net IRR (%) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | 1.90 | 1.55 | n/a | 17 |
| Q | 1.70 | n/a | 1.20 | 15 |
| R | n/a | 0.95 | 0.80 | 13 |
| S | 2.10 | 1.30 | n/a | 24 |

Which fund shows the strongest indication of potential reporting risk?

options.A: Fund S, because it reports both the highest TVPI and the highest net IRR among the four funds under review.
options.B: Fund Q, because its gap between DPI and TVPI, at 1.20x, is the largest among the four funds under review.
options.C: Fund R, because its gap between DPI and TVPI, at 1.75x, is the largest among the four funds under review.
options.D: Fund P, because its DPI of 1.55x is the highest, so more of its reported value rests on the manager’s NAV.

solution:
Fund of funds auditor ranks four buyout funds by the strength of their reporting-risk signal.

**Concept and theory**

Reporting risk is the possibility that the metrics and valuations a manager discloses do not fully reflect economic reality. The reading’s measurement tool is to compare DPI with TVPI:

DPI $= \frac{\text{Distributions}}{\text{Paid-in capital}}$ , RVPI $= \frac{\text{Residual value (NAV)}}{\text{Paid-in capital}}$ , TVPI $= \text{DPI} +$ RVPI.

DPI rests entirely on realized cash flows; TVPI depends on manager-determined NAV estimates. The gap TVPI − DPI equals RVPI, the part of reported value that is still an estimate.
